1.blurb: King Seong of Baekje, who sent the 538 Buddha gift, is the central figure of Ancient Korea Chapter 6 — the Baekje king who completed his kingdom's Buddhist conversion, moved the capital to Sabi, and was killed in 554 fighting the rival Korean kingdom of Silla. From the Korean side, the Buddha statue Seong sent to Japan was a piece of standard Baekje diplomacy: project soft power through religion to keep your neighbors as allies.

Buddhism reached Han China in the first century CE along the Silk Road from the Kushan Empire — a process explored in Han Dynasty Chapter 7. The Han received Buddhism slowly: an emperor's dream, a few foreign monks, a handful of translated sutras. By the time the religion reached Japan in 538, it had been digesting in the Chinese world for half a millennium.

Ashoka's Maurya state was the first political power to use government machinery to spread Buddhism — the topic of Maurya Empire Chapter 5. Ashoka dispatched missionary monks to Sri Lanka, Greek-controlled Bactria, and probably as far as Egypt. The infrastructure that eventually carried Buddhism to Japan a thousand years later was created by Ashoka's third-century-BCE state-Buddhist project.

The Buddha lived around 480 BCE in the late Vedic period of northern India — Vedic Period Chapter 7 covers his career and the explosion of new religious movements that emerged in the same generation. The religion that would arrive in Japan two thousand years later was already by Buddha's lifetime a reformist response to entrenched Vedic ritual practice.

The Kushan Empire of the first to third centuries CE was the political vehicle that carried Buddhism out of India and across Central Asia, creating the Silk Road monastic networks that eventually transmitted the religion to China — the story told in Post-Maurya Kingdoms Chapter 5. Without the Kushans, Buddhism would have stayed Indian.

The three Korean kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla — covered in Ancient Korea Chapter 4 — were the immediate political world the Yamato court interacted with. Baekje was Japan's closest ally and primary Buddhist conduit; Silla was Japan's regional rival; Goguryeo loomed in the north as the great power both Japan and Tang China had to consider when planning Korean policy.

The Buddhist transformation of Chinese civilization during the Six Dynasties period (Six Dynasties Chapter 5) is the precondition for everything that followed. By the time Korean Baekje sent the Buddha to Japan in 538, China had already been digesting Buddhism for four centuries, producing the great translation projects, monastic institutions, and theological literature that would all flow on through Korea to Japan.
The Buddhist crisis opens where prehistoric Japan closed — the Kofun Yamato state now forced to choose between the kami and the imported Buddha.
Buddhism, writing, and statecraft kept arriving from the Korean kingdoms — Baekje in particular the patient tutor of Asuka Japan.
Meanwhile, two centuries later: the Buddhist grip on court politics that began here would eventually push the capital to Kyoto, founded in 794 as the seat of the long Heian age.
Meanwhile, thirteen centuries later: the Meiji government of the 1870s forcibly pried Buddhism and Shinto back apart, reversing the very fusion this chapter sets in motion.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang produced exactly one female emperor, Wu Zetian, and her reign was treated as a scandalous aberration — a sharp contrast to Japan's run of empresses regnant.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang dynasty built the centralized law-code-and-ministry bureaucracy that the Yamato court would soon copy wholesale as its model for a modern state.
Meanwhile, centuries earlier: the Han opened the Silk Road by accident through Zhang Qian's failed embassy, building the trans-Eurasian route along which Buddhism itself traveled toward Japan.
Meanwhile in Korea: Goguryeo, the northern warrior kingdom, accepted Buddhism in 372, more than a century and a half before the Baekje statue reached the Yamato court.
Meanwhile in Korea: Silla, the easternmost of the three rival kingdoms, took up Buddhism last and most reluctantly, around 528 — just a decade before Japan faced the same choice.
Meanwhile in Byzantium: as the Soga and Mononobe fought over Buddha statues, Justinian I was rebuilding the Hagia Sophia and trying to reconquer the lost Roman west.
Meanwhile in Byzantium: Justinian completed the great domed Hagia Sophia in Constantinople in 537, the year before the Buddha first reached the Yamato court.
Meanwhile in Byzantium: Constantinople, the New Rome on the Bosphorus, was the seat of the eastern empire that outlived the western half by a thousand years.
Meanwhile in Persia: the Sassanid Empire was at the height of its final golden age under Khosrow I, the reforming king who was the Darius of the second Persian Empire.
Meanwhile in India: the Gupta Empire was past its political peak but its synthesis of mathematics, Sanskrit literature, and Hindu revival was spreading across south Asia.
Meanwhile in India: the Gupta golden age produced the decimal place-value system, advanced astronomy, and a Sanskrit literary renaissance that radiated outward across Asia.
Meanwhile, eight centuries earlier: the Maurya emperor Ashoka turned Indian state machinery to spreading Buddhism, launching the missionary wave that would eventually reach Japan.

2.blurb: The Sui dynasty (581–618), covered in Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 1, was the short-lived continental superpower that Shotoku Taishi was modeling Japan on. The Sui reunified China after centuries of fragmentation, built the Grand Canal, codified the Kaihuang legal system, and provided the bureaucratic template that the Twelve Cap Ranks system and Seventeen-Article Constitution were attempting to import.

Justinian I — covered in Byzantine Empire Chapter 2 — provides the cleanest cross-civilizational comparison to Shotoku Taishi. Both ruled in close partnership with strong female imperial figures (Theodora and Suiko). Both built signature monumental religious architecture (Hagia Sophia and Horyu-ji). Both attempted to import the institutional model of a more sophisticated continental neighbor. Both ran out of time before their projects could fully consolidate.

The Sassanid Empire of Persia, the dominant power of western Asia for four centuries, was at the height of its final century during Shotoku's regency — covered in Persian Empire Chapter 10. Khosrow I's Sassanid court was, like Shotoku's Yamato court, attempting to balance the import of foreign cultural and religious material against the preservation of indigenous traditions.

When the Sui collapsed in 618, the Tang dynasty inherited the Sui institutional infrastructure and pushed it further — Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 2 covers the Tang founding under Li Yuan and Li Shimin's Zhenguan-era reforms. From the founding of Horyu-ji onward, Tang China was the primary cultural model for the entire Asuka-Nara reform program.

The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople — Justinian's signature building project, covered in Byzantine Empire Chapter 2 — is the closest contemporary parallel to Horyu-ji. Both were monumental religious buildings completed within seventy years of each other (Hagia Sophia 537, Horyu-ji 607), both were attempts by middle-rank powers to build at the architectural scale of a more sophisticated continental neighbor, and both have survived as living buildings to the present day.
Shotoku's Seventeen-Article ideal of harmonious bureaucratic order parallels the contemporary Byzantine vision of a divinely-ordered Christian state.

Meanwhile in prehistoric Japan: the native cult of the kami — nature and ancestor spirits — was the indigenous spiritual tradition that would later be called Shinto, and the clans guarding it fought Buddhism's arrival.
Meanwhile in Vedic India: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught the path that — a thousand years later and a continent away — Shotoku's court was enshrining as Japan's state religion.

Meanwhile in Persia: the Sassanid Empire under Khosrow II was at its zenith, locked in the last great Roman-Persian war — and within a generation it would be swept away entirely by the Arab armies of Islam.

Meanwhile in the Roman East: Constantinople, the great walled capital Constantine founded in 330, was about to be besieged by the Persians and then assaulted by the Arabs in the wars that nearly destroyed Byzantium.
Meanwhile in Arabia: the prophet Muhammad was a young Meccan merchant during Shotoku's regency, a few years from the 610 revelation that would launch Islam.
Meanwhile in Arabia: Mecca was a caravan town and pilgrimage shrine in the Hijaz, the place where — within a few years of Horyu-ji's founding — Muhammad would begin preaching a new faith.
Meanwhile in the Roman East: Byzantium — the surviving Roman Empire ruled from Constantinople — was sliding from Justinian's high tide into the Persian and Arab wars that would halve its territory.

3.blurb: Tang Taizong's Zhenguan-era reforms, covered in Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 2, are the direct model for what Naka no Oe and Kamatari were attempting in the Taika Reform two decades later. Both rulers used a coup-and-reform sequence — Xuanwu Gate Incident of 626, Isshi Incident of 645 — followed by an aggressive program of bureaucratic centralization.

The Xuanwu Gate Incident of 626 (Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 2) was the bloody palace coup that brought Tang Taizong to power, killing his brothers and forcing his father's abdication. The structural parallel to the Isshi Incident of 645 is striking: both were coups in which a junior royal killed the senior prince to clear the way for a Tang-modeled reform program.

3.matchText: destroyed by a coalition of Tang Chinese armies
3.blurb: The destruction of Baekje in 660 — Ancient Korea Chapter 7 — is told from the Korean side as the opening move of the Great Unification War, when Tang and Silla allied to dismantle the Three Kingdoms in sequence. Goguryeo would fall in 668, and then Silla would expel Tang armies in 676 to unite the peninsula on its own terms.

The Battle of Baekgang in 663 — covered from the Silla side in Ancient Korea Chapter 7 — is the maritime engagement at the mouth of the Geum River where the Tang-Silla coalition annihilated the Yamato-Baekje fleet. The Korean accounts emphasize the strategic significance: with Japanese intervention crushed, the unification of Korea under Silla became inevitable.

3.matchText: Tang and Silla turned on each other in the post-conquest carve-up
3.blurb: After defeating Baekje and Goguryeo together, Tang and Silla turned on each other for control of the peninsula — a war Silla won by 676, expelling Tang armies and unifying Korea. Ancient Korea Chapter 7 covers the war's twists: a Silla king who alternately fought and negotiated, a Tang court that overcommitted to other frontiers, and a peninsula that emerged as a single Korean state for the first time.

The Rashidun Caliphate (the four 'rightly-guided' caliphs from 632 to 661) was contemporary with the Isshi Incident and the Taika Reform — Umayyad Caliphate Chapter 3 covers the period from the Arab side. The same years Naka no Oe was building a Tang-modeled state at Asuka, the Rashidun were destroying the Sassanid Empire and conquering Byzantine Egypt and the Levant.
The Taika Reform imported the Tang-Korean administrative model wholesale — a deliberate continental upgrade of the Japanese state.
The Taika-to-ritsuryo state is the machine that, refined, becomes the Heian court of the next narrative.
The centralized land-and-tax state built here would, centuries on, be what survived to repel the Mongol invasions.

Meanwhile in Korea: Goguryeo was the northernmost and most militarized of the peninsula's three kingdoms, a warrior state that for centuries fought Chinese dynasties to a standstill on its frontier. Together with Baekje and Silla, it sent envoys and tribute to the Yamato court — and the 645 coup was staged on the very day all three kingdoms' envoys had gathered to present that tribute.

Meanwhile in China: the Tang dynasty had just been founded and was building the most sophisticated state machine on Earth — a centralized empire of provinces, population registers, state-allocated land, and a salaried bureaucracy. This was the working model the Yamato reformers were copying when they laid out gridded capitals and drafted the Taika Edicts.

Meanwhile in China: the early Tang emperors perfected the equal-field (juntian) land system — the state owns the land, allocates plots to registered cultivators, and taxes them in grain, cloth, and labor. It was built to feed a huge bureaucracy and army, and it is exactly the system the Taika reformers tried to graft onto Japan.

Meanwhile, far earlier and far to the west: the Buddha was a north Indian teacher of the 5th century BCE whose followers built one of the world's great religions. By the time a gilt-bronze Buddha statue arrived at the Yamato court from Baekje, his teachings had travelled the length of Asia — India to Central Asia to China to Korea to Japan.

Meanwhile on Tang China's western flank: the Tibetan Empire rose into a major military power that repeatedly threatened Tang's frontier and even sacked its capital. Its pressure pulled Tang attention away from Korea in the 670s — one reason the feared Tang invasion of Japan never came.

Meanwhile in western Asia: the Sassanid Persian Empire, the dominant power for four centuries, was being overrun by the Arab conquests and destroyed between 636 and 651 — the very years Naka no Oe was building his Tang-modeled state. The contrast was the lesson: centralized states absorbed shocks, and brittle ones collapsed overnight.

Meanwhile, looking ahead: a century after Tenji built his palace at Otsu, the court would settle a few miles away at Heian-kyo — modern Kyoto — and stay there for over a thousand years. The Heian capital was the mature version of the gridded, Tang-modeled city the Asuka reformers had only sketched.

Meanwhile in China: Chang'an was the Tang capital and the largest, wealthiest, most cosmopolitan city on Earth — a million people behind walls laid out on a vast north-south grid. It was the template every Japanese capital of this era, from Naniwa to Nara, was consciously imitating.

4.blurb: Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history to formally hold the title of Huangdi — Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 2 — was contemporary with Empress Jito and ruled in much the same period. The two female monarchs offer a useful contrast: where Jito's reign was treated as institutionally normal in the Yamato pattern of female sovereigns, Wu Zetian's reign was treated as a singular aberration by every later Chinese historian.

The Tang Chinese capital at Chang'an under Emperor Xuanzong (Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 3) was the cosmopolitan reference point Hakuho-era Japanese embassies were bringing back to the Yamato court. Tang Chang'an's million-person population, multi-ethnic neighborhoods, Persian and Sogdian merchants, and Buddhist monastic networks were the model of what an East Asian imperial capital looked like.

The Umayyad Caliphate (Umayyad Caliphate Chapter 4) was the rapidly expanding Arab empire of the late seventh and early eighth centuries — by 711, Umayyad armies would conquer al-Andalus in the west and reach the Indus River in the east. The Tenmu-Jito state-formation moment in Japan was contemporary with one of the most explosive imperial expansions in world history.

Unified Silla, covered in Ancient Korea Chapter 8, was Japan's most important continental contemporary across the entire Hakuho and Nara periods. Silla's golden age (roughly 668 to 935) was a 250-year stretch of cultural flowering, Buddhist patronage, maritime trade reaching as far as the Persian Gulf, and intermittently strained relations with Japan over the Baekje refugee question.
The Yamato state matured as the Classic Maya entered collapse — the 7th–8th century reordering both ends of the world.
Meanwhile in Tang China: Chang'an was the cosmopolitan grid-capital whose layout, institutions, and Buddhist culture Yamato monks studied and brought home.
Meanwhile in early Japan: the kami worship of the Kofun-era clans — the indigenous cult of nature and ancestor spirits that crystallized into Shinto.
Meanwhile in Tang China: Chang'an, the model grid-capital — though, unlike Fujiwara-kyo, it placed the imperial palace at its northern end.
Meanwhile on the continent: the Tang dynasty at its high-water mark, the cultural and military hegemon whose bureaucratic model Japan was racing to import.
Meanwhile at the western end of Eurasia: the Heraclian-dynasty Byzantines, having survived the Arab and Persian wars, stabilizing on a smaller base around Anatolia.
Meanwhile in the Near East: the Sassanid Persian empire, whose long wars with Byzantium had just been overtaken by the Arab Muslim conquest.
Meanwhile in the Americas: the great central-Mexican city had already collapsed around 600, leaving successor cultures to inherit its world.
Meanwhile in Mesoamerica: the Maya Classic Period at full flower — rival city-states, divine kings, and monumental inscriptions at their height.
Meanwhile across Eurasia: the Silk Road at its historical peak under the Tang, the artery linking Japan's borrowed culture to Central Asia and the Mediterranean.
Meanwhile on the continent: the Tang, midway between Taizong's reforms and Wu Zetian's reign, still the East Asian hegemon Japan modeled itself on.

5.blurb: Tang Chang'an at the time of Heijo-kyo's founding was the largest city in the world (around one million residents) and the most cosmopolitan — Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 3 covers its multi-ethnic neighborhoods, Sogdian merchants, Indian Buddhist monks, and the wave of Korean and Japanese students moving through the capital. Heijo-kyo was a deliberate quarter-scale copy of this model.
The building of the Nara capital is the dress rehearsal for Heian-kyo — the grid city the next narrative opens in.
Meanwhile in China, the Tang dynasty was the institutional template the Yamato court was copying wholesale — its law codes, equal-field land system, and capital plan.
Meanwhile, the indigenous kami worship of the Japanese islands, later named Shinto, ran far deeper than the imported continental institutions layered on top of it.
Meanwhile, more than a thousand years later, the 1868 Meiji Restoration would still invoke the language and concepts of this eighth-century ritsuryo state.
Meanwhile in China, Heijo-kyo was built as a deliberate scale model of the Tang Chinese imperial city — the grid, the markets, the palace at the north end.
Meanwhile in Iberia, the same Umayyad surge that reached the Indus had conquered al-Andalus by 711 — within a year of Genmei's capital move.
Meanwhile in Francia, the Battle of Tours in 732 marked the western limit of Umayyad expansion at the Pyrenees, a generation after Nara was founded.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world, Umayyad armies had reached the Indus River and Iberia by 711, building an empire on early-Caliphate foundations just as Japan built on its Asuka reforms.
Meanwhile in Tang China, Emperor Xuanzong had just taken the throne in 712, opening the High Tang reign that Japanese embassies came to study.
Meanwhile in China, the High Tang reign of Xuanzong peaked in the great cultural moment of Li Bai and Du Fu — the model of civilization Nara was reaching toward.
Meanwhile, Persian refugees fleeing the destroyed Sassanid Empire were among the cosmopolitan crowds filling Tang Chang'an, the city Heijo-kyo imitated.
Meanwhile in Iran, the Sassanid Empire had been destroyed by the Arab conquests, scattering Persian exiles eastward toward Tang China.
Meanwhile in Korea, Silla had unified the peninsula and was entering the golden age of its consolidated kingdom.
Meanwhile in the eastern Mediterranean, the Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty was about to plunge into the Iconoclasm crisis.
Meanwhile in Byzantium, the Iconoclasm controversy over religious images was tearing the empire apart just as Nara was filling with new Buddhist temples.
Meanwhile in the Near East, the early Caliphate provided the institutional base the Umayyads built their expanding empire upon.
Meanwhile in Constantinople, the Isaurian dynasty took power in 717 and would soon launch the Byzantine assault on holy images.
Meanwhile in Korea, Unified Silla stood at the start of its golden age, the peninsula's first single ruling power.

6.blurb: The Abbasid Revolution of 750 — Islamic Golden Age Chapter 1 — overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate and established the dynasty that would build Baghdad in 762 as a planned capital on a Tang-influenced grid plan eerily similar to Heijo-kyo's. The Daibutsu was dedicated in 752, two years after the revolution; the two great planned capitals of the late eighth century were being built within a decade of each other on opposite ends of Eurasia.

Borobudur in central Java, one of the largest Buddhist monuments ever built (Srivijaya Chapter 1), was begun a generation after the Daibutsu was cast — the Southeast Asian counterpart to Japan's great state-Buddhist building project. Both monuments demonstrate the eighth-century moment when Mahayana Buddhism was being patronized at imperial scale across most of east and southeast Asia.

The Tang High Tang period of Emperor Xuanzong's reign (Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 3) is the cultural moment Ganjin sailed from. The Tang temple architecture that Toshodai-ji preserves — and that no longer exists in Tang China itself, since the original Tang wooden buildings burned down centuries ago — flowed to Japan through monks like Ganjin in the years just before the An Lushan Rebellion broke the Tang.
The Great Buddha of Nara — a state religion cast in bronze — is the Japanese counterpart to the monumental sacred projects of the Umayyad age.
Meanwhile in the Heian period: the Fujiwara intermarriage strategy reached full maturity, with the family marrying its daughters to emperors and ruling as regents for child sovereigns.
Meanwhile in India: the historical Buddha, Siddhartha Gautama, taught in the Ganges plain around the 5th century BCE — the founder whose teachings, a millennium later, anchored Japan's Nara temples.
Meanwhile in China: the Tang court was the cultural template Japan copied wholesale — its capital plan, law codes, writing, and Buddhism all flowed east to Nara.
Meanwhile in Persia: glassware and luxury goods from the Iranian world traveled the Silk Road all the way to Nara, where Persian glass still survives in the Shoso-in treasure house.
Meanwhile across Eurasia: the Silk Road overland trade network linked China to the Mediterranean, and Heijo-kyo sat at its far eastern terminus, receiving goods from across the continent.
Meanwhile in China: Tang embassies sent gifts to the Japanese court, many of which ended up preserved in the Shoso-in — a direct material trace of Sino-Japanese exchange.
Meanwhile in India: Nagarjuna, the great 2nd-century philosopher of the Madhyamaka "middle way," founded the school that Nara's Sanron tradition would carry to Japan.
Meanwhile in Europe: the Frankish kings ruled the largest realm in the post-Roman West, and their burial church at Saint-Denis was being built across the same eighth century the Daibutsu was cast.
Meanwhile in China: Chang'an, the Tang capital, was the largest city on Earth and the grid-plan model that both Heijo-kyo and Abbasid Baghdad consciously imitated.
Meanwhile in Iraq: the Abbasids would build the Great Mosque of Samarra, the largest mosque ever raised — the Islamic counterpart to the Daibutsu in this Eurasian age of monumental religion.
Meanwhile in Iraq: the Abbasids founded Baghdad in 762 as a new round caliphal capital on a Chang'an-influenced plan — built within a decade of Heijo-kyo on the opposite end of Eurasia.

7.blurb: The An Lushan Rebellion of 755–763 (Sui, Tang & Song China Chapter 4) killed perhaps 36 million people and broke the back of the Tang dynasty. By the 770s when the Hyakumanto Darani was being printed and the Dokyo Affair was unfolding, Tang China was a visibly weakening power — and the kentoshi mission that had brought Japan its institutional models for two centuries was running on diminishing returns from the Tang side.

The Dokyo Affair has a structural parallel in the Byzantine Empire's ongoing tensions between iconoclast emperors and the powerful monastic establishment — Byzantine Empire Chapter 7 covers the iconoclast century when the Byzantine state was struggling with exactly the question that Dokyo's near-coup raised in Japan: how much political power should organized monastic religion be allowed to accumulate within a state that had patronized it?

The Heian period that succeeds the Asuka-Nara periods (Heian Japan Chapter 1) covers 794 to 1185 — the brilliant aesthetic civilization centered on the new capital at Kyoto, the Fujiwara clan's regency dominance, the masterworks of Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shonagon, and the eventual rise of the warrior class that would close the classical era in the Genpei War.
Meanwhile in prehistoric Japan: the Yamato clan claimed descent from the sun goddess Amaterasu, the divine ancestry that made their rule sacred long before the Nara chroniclers wrote it down.
Meanwhile in prehistoric Japan: Shinto, the indigenous cult of the kami, was the native spiritual tradition the Soga and Mononobe clans fought over when Buddhism first arrived.
Meanwhile in Tang China: Chang'an, the cosmopolitan Tang capital, was the model Japan copied for its own grid-plan cities and the place where Abe no Nakamaro lived out his life.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Abbasid Caliphate, fresh from overthrowing the Umayyads, was building Baghdad as its new capital in the very years of the Dokyo Affair.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: Baghdad rose as the round city of the Abbasids, founded 762 and walled by 766, exactly as Nara Japan was printing its million pagodas.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Abbasid revolution had toppled the Umayyad dynasty in 750 and inaugurated the golden age centered on Baghdad.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Umayyad dynasty was the regime the Abbasids overthrew in 750, ending the first great line of caliphs.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Abbasid revolution of 750 opened the Islamic Golden Age, with Baghdad as its intellectual and political heart.
Meanwhile in Europe: Charlemagne had just inherited the Frankish throne in 768 and was beginning the conquests that would unite most of western Europe.
Meanwhile in Europe: the Frankish kingdom, soon led by Charlemagne, was consolidating into the dominant power of the Latin West.
Meanwhile in Europe: Carolingian rule under Charlemagne unified much of western Europe just before the Viking longships arrived to test its defenses.
Meanwhile in Britain: the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms had taken shape after Rome withdrew, the world that produced the epic poem Beowulf.
Meanwhile in China, the Tang dynasty — the cosmopolitan empire whose institutions, capital plan, and Buddhism Nara Japan copied wholesale — was entering the turmoil of the An Lushan Rebellion.

8.blurb: Heian-kyo, the new capital Kammu founded in 794, is the central setting of Heian Japan Chapter 1 onward. The city would remain the imperial capital for the next 1,074 years — until the Meiji Restoration in 1868 — and would be the stage for the Heian court culture, the Fujiwara regency, the brilliant women writers, and eventually the Genpei War that ended the classical period.

The Kyoto that Kammu founded as Heian-kyo became the center of one of the most refined and aesthetically obsessed court cultures in human history — Heian Japan Chapter 4 covers the Heian court aesthetic in detail. Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji, Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book, and the entire kana-script literary explosion happen in the city Kammu founded in 794.

Charlemagne was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800, six years after Kammu founded Heian-kyo — the Carolingian moment is the European structural parallel to the Heian moment. Both Kammu and Charlemagne were attempting to consolidate strong centralized monarchies after centuries of fragmentation; both founded capitals (Aachen and Heian-kyo) that would symbolize their dynastic ambitions; both used religious institutions (the Frankish church for Charlemagne, the new Heian temples for Kammu) as instruments of imperial authority.

The Viking raid on Lindisfarne in 793, one year before Kammu founded Heian-kyo, is the conventional opening of the Viking Age (Viking Age Chapter 1). The same year Japan's last classical capital was being founded, the European world was opening one of its most disruptive periods of long-distance maritime expansion — the Scandinavian raids that would reshape the political geography of England, Ireland, and the North Atlantic across the next two and a half centuries.

Harun al-Rashid (786–809), the Abbasid caliph at the height of Baghdad's golden age, was the eastern-Mediterranean contemporary of Emperor Kammu — Islamic Golden Age Chapter 2 covers his reign and the House of Wisdom translation project. The Baghdad of Harun al-Rashid and the Heian-kyo of Kammu were the two great planned capitals of the late eighth century, both at the height of their cultural production.

The samurai class that the Emishi-war military reorganization of Kammu's reign began producing would dominate Japanese politics from the late Heian period onward — Heian Japan Chapter 6 covers the rise of the warrior aristocracy. The institutional foundation laid by Kammu's abolition of the conscript army in 792 produced the warrior families whose descendants would close the classical era in the Genpei War four centuries later.
Meanwhile in Heian Japan: the move to Heian-kyo in 794 opens the next era, the brilliant court culture of The Tale of Genji and the Fujiwara regents.
Meanwhile in Meiji Japan: in 1868 the Meiji Restoration ends the warrior shogunates, restores the emperor, and moves the court from Kyoto to Edo, renamed Tokyo.
Meanwhile in Edo Japan: the Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868, the long peace of the warrior government before the Meiji Restoration.
Meanwhile in Tang China: the cosmopolitan Tang capital sat at the eastern end of the Silk Road, the trade and pilgrimage network that carried goods and Buddhism across Eurasia.
Meanwhile in Europe: Charlemagne's Carolingian empire was the great Christian power of the West, crowned by the pope in 800 just as the Viking raids began.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Abbasid Caliphate under Harun al-Rashid was at the height of its golden age, ruling from Baghdad as Kammu built Heian-kyo.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: Baghdad, the Abbasid capital, was the largest city of the Islamic world and the cultural center of the connected Eurasian middle.
Meanwhile in the Islamic world: the Islamic Golden Age of scholarship, science, and translation flourished under the Abbasids while Heian-kyo was founded.
Meanwhile in Tang China: the dynasty Japan modeled its state on had survived the An Lushan Rebellion but was visibly weakening as provincial governors grew autonomous.
Meanwhile in Korea: the Unified Silla golden age was nearing its last century, with Korean trade networks reaching as far as the Persian Gulf.
Meanwhile in Persia: the Persian Gulf was the maritime hinge of the Indian Ocean trade that linked the Islamic world to East Asia in this era.
Meanwhile in Scandinavia: the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, one year before the Heian-kyo move, opened the Viking Age of Scandinavian expansion across Europe.
Meanwhile in the Americas: the classic Maya cities of the Yucatan were approaching their mysterious collapse in the ninth and tenth centuries.
Meanwhile in the Andes: the middle-horizon empires of Wari and Tiwanaku were at their peak, the great highland powers before the Inca.
Meanwhile in the Andes: Wari was a highland empire of the Peruvian Andes at its peak during Japan's Nara period.
Meanwhile in the Andes: Tiwanaku was the great ceremonial and political center near Lake Titicaca, a peer of Wari in the Andean middle horizon.
